analysis.one_liner: Ends the carried interest tax break so fund managers' profits share is taxed like regular pay.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced by the chairman of the Senate Finance Committee himself, was referred to that committee and died there with no hearing, no markup, and no vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current law, managers of private equity, hedge fund, and real estate partnerships can defer tax on "carried interest" — a share of the fund's profits given to them as compensation — and treat it more favorably than a paycheck. This bill would instead treat that compensation as ordinary income each year, taxed at regular rates, and eliminate deferral. It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and never moved.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers, who currently make up the difference when a small group of wealthy fund managers pays lower effective rates on compensation that functions like pay. The bill would also curb deferral games where managers borrow against their partnership stakes to avoid tax for years. The revenue the change raises would broadly spread across everyone who pays into the same tax base.

how_it_helps.text: The bill eliminates the concept of carried interest and requires partners in private equity, real estate, or hedge funds to recognize deemed compensation annually, taxed at ordinary income tax rates and subject to self-employment taxation, ending the ability to defer tax until income is realized.

The bill requires the fair market value of a partnership interest received for services to be included in income at the time of transfer, closing the gap where a manager receives a stake worth millions but reports little or no current income.

The bill repeals section 1061 — the 2017 rule that only partially restricted the loophole by requiring a three-year holding period — replacing it with a full rewrite that taxes the compensation annually instead of partially.
The bill includes anti-abuse rules aimed at partnership loans to managers, tiered structures, and undervaluation of property, targeting the workarunds managers previously used to avoid taxation.

analysis.who_pays: Managers at private equity firms, hedge funds, and real estate investment partnerships, who would pay ordinary income and self-employment tax on their profit share each year instead of deferring it and often paying lower capital-gains-type treatment. Their funds would face new reporting and compliance costs.
analysis.who_pays_short: Private equity and hedge fund managers

drawbacks.text: The bill's definition of specified assets includes real estate held for rental or investment, so it reaches well beyond Wall Street buyout funds and would raise taxes on real estate partnership managers as well — a group that includes far smaller operations than mega-funds.

The deemed-compensation formula charges fund managers a minimum tax on their capital stake each year regardless of whether the fund actually made money that year, which critics would call a penalty on illiquid, long-horizon investments whose value is only realized later.

A long-standing good-faith objection to carried interest reform is that fund managers genuinely hold equity at risk rather than receiving a salary, and that raising their taxes could push fund activity and capital formation abroad — an argument industry defenders have made for decades.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is a fairer tax base: income that functions as compensation for managing other people's money would be taxed like compensation. The cost falls on a small, high-income group, which is the point — but the bill is drafted aggressively, reaching all real estate investment partnerships and imposing a minimum annual charge even in loss years, so its complexity and breadth would create real compliance burdens and winners-and-losers beyond the mega-funds its name targets.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee on day one, and the committee — chaired by the bill's own sponsor — never took it up before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Wyden introduced the bill on November 15, 2023, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance the same day.
The bill had 10 cosponsors: 8 of 48 Senate Democrats and 2 of the 4 Senate independents — no Republican cosponsors.
No further action was taken: the action history shows no hearing, no committee markup, no floor vote, and no House companion activity before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
Senator Wyden chaired the Senate Finance Committee during this Congress, meaning the committee that buried the bill was led by its sponsor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private equity, hedge fund, and real estate fund managers are better off: the tax treatment the bill targeted remained intact for the entire Congress, and no one else gains from a bill that died without a hearing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Private equity and hedge fund managers

for.name: Sen. Ron Wyden
for.role: U.S. Senator from Oregon; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Ending the Carried Interest Loophole Act in the Senate.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee (118th Congress)
against.role: Committee of referral; chaired by the bill's sponsor
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill — no hearing, no markup, no vote — after referral on the day of introduction, letting it die when the Congress ended.

against.name: Private equity and hedge fund industry
against.what_they_did: Have long and effectively opposed carried interest tax increases in Congress, defending the current treatment across multiple Congresses and administrations.

sides.party_line_note: All 10 cosponsors were Democrats or independents; no Republican signed on, and the bill never reached a vote where party splits would be recorded.

industries.industry: Private equity and hedge fund managers
industries.note: The bill would tax their carried-interest profit share as ordinary compensation each year instead of allowing deferral and more favorable treatment, directly raising their tax bills. Their interest in keeping the current treatment runs against the broader taxpaying public, who bear the cost of the narrowed tax base.

industries.industry: Real estate investment and rental partnerships
industries.note: Rental and investment real estate is squarely within the bill's definition of specified assets, so real estate partnership managers would also lose the carried-interest treatment. Keeping profits-share income taxed lightly shifts the tax load onto other taxpayers.

industries.industry: Fund administration and tax advisory services
industries.note: The bill's new deemed-compensation calculations, reporting requirements, and anti-abuse regulations would create heavy new compliance work — a cost to fund clients, but new billable business for the accountants and lawyers who serve the industry.
